label: Phaedo · The Final Argument
title: The Final Argument
paragraphs: Very well, said Socrates. Harmonia of Thebes, it seems, has in a way been fairly well appeased for us. But what of Cadmus, Cebes? he said. How shall we appease him, and with what argument?

I think you will find a way, said Cebes. This argument against the attunement, at any rate, you put astonishingly well, beyond what I expected. For while Simmias was telling us what puzzled him, I wondered very much whether anyone would be able to do anything with his argument; so it seemed very strange to me that it failed at once to withstand the first assault of your argument. I would not be surprised, then, if the same thing happened to the argument of Cadmus too.

My good friend, said Socrates, do not talk big, or some evil eye may overturn the argument that is about to come. But that will be the god's concern. Let us close in, in Homer's fashion, and test whether there is anything in what you say.

The sum of what you are asking is this. You require it to be shown that our soul is imperishable and immortal, if a man who is a philosopher and is about to die, who is confident and believes that after death he will fare far better there than if he had lived a different life to its end, is not to be confident with a senseless and foolish confidence. As for showing that the soul is something strong and godlike, and that it existed even earlier, before we became human beings, you say nothing prevents all this from pointing not to immortality, but only to this: that soul is long-lasting, and existed somewhere before for an immeasurable length of time, and knew and did all sorts of things. But it was no more immortal for that. Its very coming into a human body was the beginning of its perishing, like a disease; it lives this life in hardship, and at the end it perishes in what is called death. And you say it makes no difference whether it comes into a body once or many times, at least as far as the fear each of us feels is concerned; for anyone who does not know that it is immortal, and cannot give an account to show it, ought to be afraid, unless he is senseless.
That, I think, Cebes, is roughly what you are saying. I go over it more than once on purpose, so that nothing may escape us, and so that you may add something or take something away, if you wish.
No, said Cebes, for the present there's nothing I need to take away or add. That is what I am saying.

Then Socrates paused for a long time, considering something within himself. It is no small thing you are asking for, Cebes, he said. For we must deal thoroughly with the cause of coming to be and of destruction in general. So I will tell you, if you like, what happened to me in these matters. Then, if anything I say seems useful to you, you will use it to win conviction about the things you speak of.
Indeed I would like that, said Cebes.

Then listen, and I will tell you. When I was young, Cebes, he said, I had an astonishing desire for that wisdom which they call the inquiry into nature. It seemed to me a magnificent thing to know the causes of each thing: why each thing comes to be, why it perishes, and why it is. And I often turned myself this way and that, examining first questions like these: Is it when the hot and the cold take on a kind of rot, as some used to say, that living creatures are bred? And is it blood that we think with, or air, or fire? Or is it none of these, but the brain that supplies the senses of hearing and sight and smell, and from these come memory and belief, and from memory and belief, when they have come to rest, in this way knowledge comes to be? Then again I examined how these things are destroyed, and what happens to the sky and the earth, until in the end I decided that I was as ungifted for this kind of inquiry as anything could be.

I will give you proof enough. The things I had known clearly before, at least as I myself and others thought, I was then so thoroughly blinded to by this inquiry that I unlearned even what I had thought I knew before, about many other things and about why a human being grows. Before, I thought it was plain to everyone that it is through eating and drinking. For when, from food, flesh is added to flesh and bone to bone, and by the same account what belongs to each of the other parts is added to it, then the bulk that was small has later become large, and so the small human being becomes a large one. That is what I thought then. Does it not seem reasonable to you?
It does to me, said Cebes.

Then consider this too. I thought my belief was good enough when a large man standing beside a small one appeared larger just by a head, and one horse larger than another. And clearer still than these: ten seemed to me more than eight because two had been added to it, and the two-cubit length larger than the one-cubit because it exceeded it by half of itself.
And now, said Cebes, what do you think about them?

By Zeus, he said, I am far from thinking that I know the cause of any of these things. I do not even accept from myself that when someone adds one to one, either the one it was added to has become two, or the one that was added, or that the one added and the one it was added to became two because of the adding of the one to the other. For I find it strange that when each of them was apart from the other, each was one and they were not then two, but when they came near each other, this became the cause of their becoming two: the meeting that consists in being put near each other. Nor can I any longer be persuaded that if someone splits one, this in its turn, the splitting, has become the cause of there being two. For the cause of becoming two turns out to be the opposite of the earlier one. Then it was that they were brought near each other and one was added to the other; now it is that one is taken away and separated from the other. Nor do I any longer persuade myself that I know why one comes to be, or, in a word, why anything else comes to be or perishes or is, by this way of proceeding. Instead I muddle along at random with another way of my own, and this one I do not accept at all.

But one day I heard someone reading from a book, as he said, by Anaxagoras, and saying that it is mind that orders all things and is the cause of all things. I was delighted with this cause, and it seemed to me in a way right that mind should be the cause of all things. And I thought that, if this is so, mind in ordering all things orders them and places each thing in whatever way is best. So if anyone wished to find the cause of each thing, how it comes to be or perishes or is, what he had to find out about it was this: how it is best for it to be, or to undergo or do anything else. On this account, then, a person ought to examine nothing else, about that thing itself or about the others, than what is most excellent and best. And the same person must necessarily know the worse as well; for the knowledge of both is the same.

Reasoning in this way, I was glad to think I had found in Anaxagoras a teacher of the cause of things after my own mind. I thought he would tell me first whether the earth is flat or round, and when he had told me, would go on to explain the cause and the necessity, saying what was better, and that it was better for it to be so. And if he said it was in the center, he would go on to explain that it was better for it to be in the center. If he made these things clear to me, I was prepared to long no more for any other form of cause. And I was prepared to ask in just the same way about the sun and the moon and the other stars, about their speeds relative to one another and their turnings and whatever else happens to them: how it is better for each of them to do and to undergo what it undergoes. For I never thought that, when he said they were ordered by mind, he would bring in any other cause for them than that it is best for them to be just as they are. So I thought that in assigning the cause to each of them and to all in common, he would go on to explain what is best for each and what is the common good of all. I would not have sold my hopes for a great price. I got hold of the books in all eagerness and read them as fast as I could, so that I might know as soon as possible the best and the worse.

From that wonderful hope, my friend, I was swept away. For as I went on reading I saw a man making no use of mind and assigning to it no causes for the ordering of things, but giving as causes airs and ethers and waters and many other strange things. It seemed to me that he was in just the same case as someone who said that Socrates does everything he does by mind, and then, when he tried to give the causes of each thing I do, said first that I am sitting here now because my body is made up of bones and sinews; and the bones are hard and have joints that separate them from one another, while the sinews are such as to tighten and slacken, and they wrap around the bones together with the flesh and the skin that holds them together; so, as the bones swing in their sockets, the sinews by slackening and tightening make me able, I suppose, to bend my limbs now, and that is the cause of my sitting here with my legs bent. And again, about my talking with you, he would give other causes of the same kind — voices and airs and hearings and countless other such things — and would neglect to state the true causes: that since the Athenians thought it better to vote against me, for that reason I in my turn have thought it better to sit here, and more just to stay and undergo whatever penalty they order. For, by the dog, I think these sinews and bones would long ago have been somewhere near Megara or among the Boeotians, carried there by a belief about what is best, if I had not thought it more just and more honorable to undergo whatever penalty the city imposes rather than to escape and run away.

But to call such things causes is too strange. If someone said that without having such things, bones and sinews and whatever else I have, I would not be able to do what I have decided, he would be telling the truth. But to say that it is because of them that I do what I do, and this while acting by mind, and not by my choice of what is best — that would be a great and far-reaching carelessness of speech. Think of not being able to distinguish that the real cause is one thing, and that without which the cause could never be a cause is another. It is this that most people seem to me to be groping for as if in the dark, using a name that belongs to something else, when they call it a cause. That is why one man puts a whirl around the earth and has the earth kept in place by the sky, while another props it on air as a base, like a flat kneading trough. But the power by which things are now placed in the best way they could be placed — this they neither look for nor think to have any divine strength. They believe they will someday discover an Atlas stronger and more immortal than this one, and better at holding everything together; and that it is what is good and binding that truly binds and holds things together, they do not think at all.

I would most gladly become anyone's pupil to learn how such a cause works. But since I was deprived of it, and was able neither to find it myself nor to learn it from another, do you want me, Cebes, he said, to show you how I have carried out my second voyage in search of the cause?
I want that more than I can tell you, he said.

Well then, he said, after this, when I had given up examining the things that are, I decided I must take care not to suffer what happens to people who watch and examine the sun in an eclipse. For some of them, I believe, ruin their eyes, unless they examine its image in water or something of that kind. I had something like that in mind, and I was afraid my soul would be blinded altogether if I looked at things with my eyes and tried to grasp them with each of my senses. So I decided I must take refuge in arguments and examine in them the truth of the things that are. Perhaps my comparison is, in a way, not a likeness. For I do not at all grant that someone who examines the things that are in arguments is examining them in images any more than someone who examines them in facts. However that may be, this is the way I set out. On each occasion I lay down as my hypothesis the argument I judge to be strongest, and whatever seems to me to agree with it I put down as true, both about cause and about all other things, and whatever does not, as not true. But I want to tell you more clearly what I mean; for I think you do not understand now.
No, by Zeus, said Cebes, not very well.

This is what I mean, he said. It is nothing new, but what I have never stopped saying, both at other times and in the argument just past. I am going to try to show you the form of cause I have worked at, and I go back to those much-repeated things and begin from them, laying down as my hypothesis that there is something beautiful itself by itself, and good, and large, and all the rest. If you grant me these and agree that they exist, I hope from them to show you the cause, and to discover that the soul is immortal.
You may take it that I grant you this, said Cebes, so lose no time in finishing.

Then consider what comes next, he said, and see whether you think as I do. It seems to me that if anything else is beautiful besides the beautiful itself, it is beautiful for no other reason at all than that it shares in that beautiful; and I say the same of everything. Do you agree to a cause of this kind?
I agree, he said.

Then I no longer understand those other wise causes, he said, and I cannot recognize them. If someone tells me that anything is beautiful because it has a bright color, or a shape, or anything else of that kind, I let all that go — for all the rest confuses me — and I keep this by me, simply and plainly and perhaps foolishly: that nothing else makes it beautiful but the presence of that beautiful, or its association with it, or whatever the way and manner in which it has come to it. For I do not go so far as to insist on that, but only that it is by the beautiful that all beautiful things are beautiful. This seems to me the safest answer to give, both to myself and to anyone else. If I hold on to this I think I will never fall; it is safe for me and for anyone else to answer that it is by the beautiful that beautiful things are beautiful. Or do you not think so too?
I do.
And so it is by largeness that large things are large and larger things larger, and by smallness that smaller things are smaller?
Yes.

Then you too would not accept it if someone said that one man is larger than another by a head, and that the smaller is smaller by that same thing. You would protest that you for your part say nothing else than this: that everything larger than another is larger by nothing but largeness, and is larger because of this, because of largeness; and that the smaller is smaller by nothing but smallness, and is smaller because of this, because of smallness. You would be afraid, I think, that some opposing argument would meet you if you said that someone is larger and smaller by a head: first, that the larger is larger and the smaller smaller by the same thing; and then, that the larger man is larger by a head, which is small, and that this is a monstrous thing, for someone to be large by something small. Or would you not be afraid of that?
Cebes laughed. I would, he said.

Then, he said, you would be afraid to say that ten is more than eight by two, and exceeds it for that cause, and not by multitude and because of multitude? And that the two-cubit length is larger than the one-cubit by half, and not by largeness? For the fear is surely the same.
Certainly, he said.

And again: when one is added to one, would you not be wary of saying that the adding is the cause of there coming to be two, or when one is split, the splitting? You would cry out loud that you know of no other way in which each thing comes to be than by sharing in the particular being of each thing it shares in; and that in these cases you have no other cause of coming to be two than sharing in twoness, and that whatever is going to be two must share in this, and whatever is going to be one must share in oneness. As for these splittings and addings and other such subtleties, you would let them go, and leave them for those wiser than yourself to answer with. But you, afraid of your own shadow, as the saying goes, and of your inexperience, would hold on to that safety of the hypothesis and answer accordingly.

And if anyone fastened on the hypothesis itself, you would let him go and would not answer until you had examined the things that follow from it, to see whether in your view they agree or disagree with one another. And when you had to give an account of the hypothesis itself, you would give it in the same way, laying down another hypothesis in its turn, whichever of the higher ones seemed best, until you came to something sufficient. And you would not jumble things together as the disputers do, by talking at the same time about the starting point and about the things that follow from it, if you wanted to find any of the things that are. For they, perhaps, give not one word or one thought to this; their wisdom makes them able to stir everything up together and still be pleased with themselves. But you, if you are one of the philosophers, would do, I think, as I say.
That's very true, said Simmias and Cebes together.
ECHECRATES: By Zeus, Phaedo, they had good reason. It seems to me that he made these things astonishingly clear, even to someone with only a little sense.
PHAEDO: Very much so, Echecrates, and so it seemed to all who were there.
ECHECRATES: And to us who were not there and are hearing it now. But what was said after that?

PHAEDO: I think that when this had been granted him, and it was agreed that each of the forms is something, and that the other things, by coming to share in them, take their names from these very forms, he next asked: If that is what you say, then when you say that Simmias is larger than Socrates but smaller than Phaedo, are you not saying that both are in Simmias at that moment, largeness and smallness?
I am.

But you agree, he said, that the statement that Simmias exceeds Socrates is not true in the way the words put it? For surely it is not Simmias' nature to exceed him by this, by being Simmias, but by the largeness he happens to have. Nor again does he exceed Socrates because Socrates is Socrates, but because Socrates has smallness in relation to his largeness?
True.
Nor again is he exceeded by Phaedo because Phaedo is Phaedo, but because Phaedo has largeness in relation to Simmias' smallness?
That is so.

So that is how Simmias comes to be called both small and large, being between the two: to the one he submits his smallness, to be exceeded by that one's largeness, and to the other he presents his largeness, which exceeds that one's smallness.
And he smiled as he spoke. It seems I am going to talk like a written contract, he said; but still, it is surely as I say.
He agreed.

I say this because I want you to think as I do. For it seems to me that not only is largeness itself never willing to be large and small at once, but also the largeness in us never admits the small and is not willing to be exceeded. One of two things happens: either it flees and withdraws when its opposite, the small, approaches it, or, when that has come, it has perished. It is not willing to stand its ground and admit smallness and so be other than what it was. I, for instance, have admitted smallness and stood my ground, and while still being who I am, I am this same man, small. But that largeness has not dared, being large, to be small. In the same way the small in us is never willing to become or to be large, nor is any other of the opposites, while still being what it was, willing at the same time to become and to be its opposite. Either it goes away or it perishes when this happens to it.
That is exactly how it appears to me, said Cebes.

Then one of those present, when he heard this — who it was I do not clearly remember — said: By the gods, was not the very opposite of what is now being said agreed in our earlier arguments, that the larger comes to be from the smaller and the smaller from the larger, and that this simply is how opposites come to be, from their opposites? But now it seems to me to be said that this could never happen.

Socrates turned his head toward him and listened. You have done bravely to remind us, he said, but you do not see the difference between what is being said now and what was said then. Then it was said that an opposite thing comes to be from an opposite thing; now, that the opposite itself could never become opposite to itself, neither the one in us nor the one in nature. Then, my friend, we were speaking about the things that have the opposites, calling them by the names of those opposites; now we are speaking about those opposites themselves, which, by being in them, give the things named their names. And these themselves, we say, would never be willing to admit coming to be from one another.
At the same time he looked at Cebes and said: Surely, Cebes, none of what he said has troubled you too?
No, not this time, said Cebes; though I don't say there aren't many things that trouble me.
Then we have agreed on this without qualification, he said: that an opposite will never be opposite to itself.
Entirely, he said.
Now consider this too, he said, and see whether you will agree. Is there something you call hot, and something you call cold?
There is.
The same as what you call snow and fire?
By Zeus, no.
The hot is something different from fire, and the cold something different from snow?
Yes.

But this much, I think, you do believe: that snow, being snow, will never admit the hot, as we were saying before, and still be what it was, snow and hot. When the hot approaches, it will either withdraw from it or perish.
Certainly.
And fire, in its turn, when the cold approaches it, will either get out of the way or perish; it will never dare to admit coldness and still be what it was, fire and cold.
That's true, he said.

So it is the case, he said, with some things of this kind, that not only is the form itself entitled to its own name for all time, but so is something else as well, which is not that, but always has the form of that, whenever it exists. Perhaps what I mean will be clearer in this example. The odd must surely always get this name that we are now using — or not?
Certainly.

Is it the only one of the things that are — for this is my question — or is there something else too, which is not the same as the odd, but which we must nevertheless always call odd as well, along with its own name, because its nature is such that it is never parted from the odd? I mean the sort of thing that happens to the number three and to many others. Consider the number three. Does it not seem to you that it must always be called both by its own name and by the name of the odd, though the odd is not the same as the number three? Yet the number three and the number five and the whole half of number are of such a nature that, though not the same as the odd, each of them is always odd. And again two and four and the whole other row of number, though not the same as the even, are nevertheless each of them always even. Do you agree or not?
Of course, he said.

Then look at what I want to make clear, he said. It is this: it appears that not only do those opposites not admit one another, but also the things that are not opposites of one another yet always have the opposites in them — these too, it seems, do not admit the form that is opposite to the one in them; when it comes upon them they either perish or withdraw. Or shall we not say that three will perish or undergo anything whatever sooner than stand its ground and become even while still being three?
Very much so, said Cebes.
And yet, he said, the number two is not opposite to the number three.
No, it isn't.
So it is not only the opposite forms that do not stand their ground when one comes upon the other; there are other things too that do not stand their ground when the opposites come upon them.
That's very true, he said.
Then do you want us, he said, to define what sort of things these are, if we can?
Certainly.
Then, Cebes, he said, would they be these: things that compel whatever they take possession of not only to have their own form, but always the form of some opposite as well?
How do you mean?
As we were saying just now. You know, surely, that whatever the form of three takes possession of must be not only three but also odd.
Certainly.
To such a thing, we say, the form opposite to the form that produces this could never come.
No.
And what produced it was the form of the odd?
Yes.
And opposite to this is the form of the even?
Yes.
So the form of the even will never come to three.
Of course not.
Then three has no share in the even.
None.
So the number three is uneven.
Yes.

Now, what I said we were to define: what sort of things, though not opposite to something, nevertheless do not admit it, the opposite. Just now, for instance, the number three, though not opposite to the even, does not admit it any the more for that, since it always brings along the opposite of the even, and the number two brings the opposite of the odd, and fire the opposite of the cold, and so with a great many others. Well, see whether you would define it this way: not only does an opposite not admit its opposite, but also that which brings along some opposite to whatever it comes to — the very thing that brings it never admits the opposite of what is brought. Go over it once more; for it does no harm to hear a thing many times. Five will not admit the form of the even, nor will ten, its double, admit the form of the odd. Now this is itself opposite to something else, yet it will not admit the form of the odd. Nor will one and a half, or the other things of that kind, the half, admit the form of the whole; nor again a third and everything of that kind — if you follow and agree that it is so.
I agree entirely, he said, and I follow.

Then tell me again from the beginning, he said. And do not answer me in the words of my question, but follow my example. I say this because, beyond that answer I spoke of at first, the safe one, I see from what is now being said another kind of safety. For if you ask me what it is that, by coming to be in a body, makes it hot, I will not give you that safe, ignorant answer, that it is heat, but a more subtle one drawn from what we have just said: that it is fire. And if you ask what it is that, by coming to be in a body, makes it sick, I will not say that it is sickness, but fever. And if you ask what it is that, by coming to be in a number, makes it odd, I will not say oddness, but oneness; and so on. See whether by now you know well enough what I want.
Quite well enough, he said.
Then answer, he said: what is it that, by coming to be in a body, makes it living?
Soul, he said.
And is this always so?
Of course, he said.
So whatever soul takes possession of, it always comes to that thing bringing life?
It does, he said.
And is there an opposite to life, or none?
There is, he said.
What?
Death.
Then soul will never admit the opposite of what it always brings along, as has been agreed from what went before?
Most decidedly, said Cebes.
Well then, what did we just now call that which does not admit the form of the even?
Uneven, he said.
And that which does not admit the just, and whatever does not admit the musical?
Unmusical, he said, and the other unjust.
Very well. And what do we call whatever does not admit death?
Immortal, he said.
And soul does not admit death?
No.
So soul is immortal.
Immortal.
Very well, he said. Shall we say this has been proved? What do you think?
Yes, and quite sufficiently, Socrates.
Well then, Cebes, he said: if the uneven were necessarily imperishable, would three not be imperishable?
Of course.

And if the unhot too were necessarily imperishable, then whenever someone brought heat against snow, the snow would get out of the way safe and unmelted? For it would not have perished, nor again would it have stood its ground and admitted the heat.
That's true, he said.
In the same way, I think, if the uncoolable were imperishable, then whenever something cold came upon fire, the fire would never be put out or perish, but would go away safe and be gone.
It must be, he said.

Then must we not say the same about the immortal? he said. If the immortal is also imperishable, it is impossible for soul to perish when death comes upon it. For by what has been said it will not admit death, and will not be dead, just as three, we said, will not be even, nor will the odd, and fire will not be cold, nor will the heat in the fire. But, someone might say, what prevents the odd, while it does not become even when the even comes upon it, as has been agreed, from perishing, and the even from having come to be in its place? Against someone who said this we could not maintain that it does not perish; for the uneven is not imperishable. If that had been agreed by us, we could easily maintain that when the even comes upon them the odd and three go away and are gone. And we could maintain the same about fire and the hot and the rest. Could we not?
Very much so.
So now, too, about the immortal: if it is agreed by us that it is also imperishable, then soul, besides being immortal, would be imperishable as well. If not, another argument would be needed.
None is needed, he said, as far as that goes. For hardly anything else could fail to admit destruction, if the immortal, which is everlasting, is going to admit destruction.
And the god, I think, said Socrates, and the form of life itself, and anything else that is immortal, would be agreed by everyone never to perish.
By everyone indeed, by Zeus, he said — by human beings, and still more, I think, by the gods.
Then since the immortal is also indestructible, would soul, if it really is immortal, not be imperishable as well?
It most certainly must be.
So when death comes upon a human being, the mortal part of him, it seems, dies, but the immortal part goes away and is gone, safe and indestructible, having withdrawn from death.
It appears so.
Then beyond all doubt, Cebes, he said, soul is immortal and imperishable, and our souls really will exist in Hades.

For my part, Socrates, he said, I have nothing else to say against this, and no way to doubt the arguments. But if Simmias here or anyone else has something to say, he would do well not to keep silent; for I do not know to what other occasion than the present one anyone could put it off, if he wants to say or hear anything about such matters.

Indeed, said Simmias, I myself no longer have any way to doubt, at least on the strength of what has been said. But because of the greatness of the things the arguments are about, and because I think little of human weakness, I am compelled still to keep some doubt in my own mind about what has been said.

Not only that, Simmias, said Socrates. You are right in what you say, and besides, the first hypotheses, even if you find them trustworthy, must still be examined more clearly. And if you work through them sufficiently, you will, I think, follow the argument as far as a human being can follow it; and if this very thing becomes clear, you will seek nothing further.
That's true, he said.

divergences.phrase: τὸν δεύτερον πλοῦν ἐπὶ τὴν τῆς αἰτίας ζήτησιν
divergences.older: the second best mode of enquiring into the cause
divergences.lectio: my second voyage in search of the cause
divergences.note: The Greek is a sailor's phrase: when the wind fails, you take to the oars. Jowett's ‘second best’ settles in advance a question Socrates leaves open, since at 100a he denies that looking at things in arguments is looking at mere images.

divergences.phrase: ἡ ἐκείνου τοῦ καλοῦ εἴτε παρουσία εἴτε κοινωνία εἴτε ὅπῃ δὴ καὶ ὅπως προσγενομένη
divergences.older: the presence and participation of beauty in whatever way or manner obtained
divergences.lectio: the presence of that beautiful, or its association with it, or whatever the way and manner in which it has come to it
divergences.note: Socrates offers three alternatives and refuses to choose among them; Jowett joins the first two with ‘and’ and turns the beautiful itself into ‘beauty’. We keep the three ‘or’s and the same words, ‘that beautiful’, used for it throughout.

divergences.phrase: ὁ δέ γε θεὸς οἶμαι, ἔφη ὁ Σωκράτης, καὶ αὐτὸ τὸ τῆς ζωῆς εἶδος
divergences.older: all men will agree that God, and the essential form of life
divergences.lectio: And the god, I think, said Socrates, and the form of life itself
divergences.note: Plato writes ‘the god’ with the article, and Cebes answers at once about ‘the gods’; Jowett's capital brings in a later faith. ‘The form of life itself’ keeps εἶδος as ‘form’, the word the whole argument has turned on.
